lessons.title: Why European Stocks Trade Cheaper: Sectors, Growth, and the Euro

children.text: In November 2024, European shares traded at a record 41% discount to US shares on forward earnings. Fund managers called Europe "uninvestable". Then came two strong years: the DAX rose 23% in 2025, European earnings jumped 24.1% in the second quarter of 2026, and by August 2026 the gap had narrowed to about 26%. The STOXX Europe 600 still trades at roughly 14.6 times next year's earnings, while the S&P 500 trades at about 19 times and the Nifty 50 at about 20 times its past year's earnings. So is Europe a bargain, or is it cheap for good reasons? Answering that question well is one of the most useful skills any investor, Indian or otherwise, can build.

body.text: A low P/E is not automatically a bargain. Europe trades cheaper mainly because of what it owns, how fast its profits grow, how much profit it earns on its capital, and the risks around its currency, energy and politics. Some of the discount is deserved. Some of it is sentiment.

markDefs.definition: Price divided by analysts' estimated earnings for the next 12 months. It looks ahead, unlike a trailing P/E, which uses the past 12 months of actual earnings.
Price divided by the last 12 months of reported earnings. NSE publishes the Nifty 50's trailing P/E daily.

. Indian investors usually see the Nifty's
. When earnings are growing, a forward P/E is lower than the trailing P/E for the same index, so mixing the two makes a market look cheaper or dearer than it really is.

body.caption: How to measure how much cheaper one market is than another

body.title: Measure the gap yourself
body.prompt: Using the figures above, the STOXX Europe 600 trades at 14.6x forward earnings and the S&P 500 at 19.1x. What is Europe's valuation discount to the US, in percent? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Discount = (1 − 14.6 ÷ 19.1) × 100 = (1 − 0.7644) × 100 = 23.6%. Reuters, using LSEG data, quoted a 26% discount in August 2026. The difference comes from different data providers, dates and definitions of US equities. That is normal. Always check the source and date before quoting a valuation gap.

children.text: The single biggest reason for Europe's discount is sector mix. The S&P 500 is dominated by technology companies with high margins, fast growth and huge global scale, and investors pay high multiples for them. Europe's indices are heavy in banks, insurers, energy, industrials and consumer staples, which the market values at lower multiples everywhere in the world, including in India. Europe's most valuable company, ASML, is worth roughly $660 to $690 billion. Nvidia alone is worth about $5.4 trillion.

body.caption: Illustrative sector P/Es applied to two different sector mixes
A simplified weighted average; official index P/Es use total price divided by total earnings

body.title: Same sectors, different index P/E
body.prompt: Using the illustrative table, calculate the simplified P/E of the Europe-style index: 9% at 28x, 26% at 11x and 65% at 17x. Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Europe-style P/E ≈ (0.09 × 28) + (0.26 × 11) + (0.65 × 17) = 2.52 + 2.86 + 11.05 = 16.43x. The US-style index works out to (0.38 × 28) + (0.12 × 11) + (0.50 × 17) = 10.64 + 1.32 + 8.50 = 20.46x. Every sector is priced identically in both, yet the Europe-style index looks about 20% cheaper purely because of what it owns. That part of the discount is not a bargain at all.

body.text: India faces the same trap in reverse. The Nifty 50 has a large weight in banks and financials, which usually trade at lower P/Es, yet the Nifty still trades near 20x. That tells you investors pay a premium for Indian companies across sectors, not just for a tech-heavy mix. Always ask whether a market is cheap sector by sector, or just cheap because of its sector mix.

markDefs.definition: The P/E ratio divided by the expected annual earnings growth rate in percent. A PEG near 1 suggests the price is roughly in line with growth; a higher PEG means you pay more for each unit of growth.

children.text: Investors pay more for companies whose profits grow faster. Over the past two decades, Europe's economy and its corporate earnings have grown more slowly than America's, held back by ageing populations, weaker productivity growth and fewer fast-scaling technology platforms. Europe did deliver strong recent results, with second-quarter 2026 earnings up 24.1% year on year according to LSEG I/B/E/S, its best quarter since 2022. But one strong quarter does not change a long-term growth reputation. The
is a simple way to see whether a low P/E is really cheap once growth is considered.

body.title: Which one is really cheaper?
body.question: Illustrative figures: a European bank trades at 9x earnings with expected growth of 4% a year. A US software company trades at 30x with expected growth of 20% a year. Which is cheaper on a PEG basis?
options: The European bank, because 9x is far lower than 30x
The US software company, with a PEG of 1.5 against the bank's 2.25
Both are equally priced, because both have single-digit PEGs
PEG cannot be used to compare companies in different countries
body.explanation: Bank PEG = 9 ÷ 4 = 2.25. Software PEG = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5. On growth-adjusted terms, the US company is cheaper despite its much higher P/E. PEG has limits: it ignores dividends, balance sheet risk and how reliable the growth forecast is. Banks often pay large dividends, which PEG does not capture. But it shows why a low P/E alone proves nothing.

children.text: Reason 3: Lower Profitability and a Different Way of Paying Shareholders

markDefs.definition: Return on equity. Net profit divided by shareholders' equity. It measures how much profit a company generates from each rupee, euro or dollar of shareholders' capital.

children.text: US companies, on average, earn a higher

than European companies, and MSCI notes that this profitability gap is one structural reason for Europe's discount. A business that earns more on every unit of capital deserves a higher price relative to its book value. The two markets also reward shareholders differently. US companies lean heavily on share buybacks. European companies pay a larger share of profits as dividends, although European buybacks have grown fast too.

body.caption: Why higher profitability supports a higher price-to-book ratio

body.title: Profitability shows up in price-to-book
body.prompt: Illustrative figures: a European company earns an ROE of 12% and trades at 14x earnings. What is its price-to-book ratio? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: P/B = ROE × P/E = 0.12 × 14 = 1.68x. A US company with an ROE of 20% at 20x earnings would trade at 0.20 × 20 = 4.0x book. The US company looks more than twice as expensive on book value, but much of that is simply higher profitability. The Nifty 50's P/B of about 3x in August 2026 reflects the relatively high ROE of India's large companies.

children.text: Reason 4: The Euro, Energy, Rates and Politics

Europe carries risks that investors demand compensation for. It imports much of its energy, so energy price spikes hit its manufacturers hard. In 2026, rising energy prices linked to conflict in the Middle East pushed eurozone inflation up, and the European Central Bank raised its deposit rate by 0.25 percentage points to 2.50%, effective 16 September 2026, while forecasting 3.0% inflation for the year. Higher rates make future earnings worth less today. Add fragmented capital markets, political instability in countries like France, heavier regulation and a smaller culture of household equity investing, and part of the discount starts to look rational.

body.label: ECB deposit facility rate
body.context: A 25 basis point hike, with the ECB keeping its 2026 inflation forecast at 3.0%. EUR/USD traded near 1.16 around the decision.

columns.label: Reasons the discount may be deserved
points: Sector mix tilted to banks, energy and industrials
Slower long-term earnings and economic growth
Energy dependence and exposure to energy price shocks
Fragmented markets, regulation and political risk

columns.label: Reasons the discount could narrow
points: Germany's 2025 reform of its debt brake, including a €500 billion infrastructure fund and higher defence spending
Strong recent earnings, up 24.1% in Q2 2026
Companies with global leadership, such as ASML, Novo Nordisk and LVMH
Investors seeking diversification away from a concentrated US market

body.text: Beware the value trap. A market or stock that is cheap for structural reasons can stay cheap for decades. European stocks traded at a discount to US stocks for most of the past 20 years, and investors who bought purely because Europe "looked cheap" often watched the gap widen further. Cheapness needs a catalyst, such as faster earnings growth or policy change, before it turns into returns.

body.title: Name the ratio
body.textWithBlank: A ratio that divides the P/E by the expected earnings growth rate, used to adjust valuation for growth, is called the ___ ratio.
body.explanation: The PEG ratio divides P/E by expected annual earnings growth in percent. It helps explain why a high-growth market can justify a higher P/E than a slow-growth one.

body.title: "Europe is a steal"
body.scenario: A friend who invests through Zerodha and an overseas brokerage account says: "Europe trades at 14.6 times earnings, the US at 19 and India at 20. Europe is obviously the cheapest. I am moving most of my money into a European ETF."
body.prompt: Explain what your friend is missing, and what they should check before deciding whether Europe is genuinely undervalued.
body.modelAnswer:
What your friend is missing:
1. Like-for-like comparison: Europe's 14.6x and the US 19.1x are forward P/Es, while the Nifty's 20.2x is a trailing P/E. They are not directly comparable.
2. Sector mix: Europe is heavy in banks, energy and industrials, which trade at lower P/Es everywhere. Part of the discount disappears when you compare sector by sector.
3. Growth: Slower long-term earnings growth justifies a lower P/E. A PEG comparison may show Europe is not as cheap as it looks.
4. Profitability: Lower average ROE supports lower valuations.
5. Risks: Energy dependence, rising ECB rates, political instability and currency swings in the euro against the rupee.
6. Concentration: Moving "most" money into one region is a diversification mistake in itself.

What to check:
1. Sector-neutral valuations comparing European and US companies in the same industries.
2. Forward earnings growth estimates for each region.
3. ROE and dividend yield alongside P/E.
4. Whether there is a catalyst, such as German fiscal spending or earnings upgrades.
5. Overseas investing rules, costs and taxes under LRS before investing from India.

body.title: Before calling any market cheap
steps: Confirm whether each P/E is forward or trailing, and from which source and date.
Compare sector weights and, where possible, sector-by-sector P/Es.
Check expected earnings growth and calculate a rough PEG.
Look at ROE, dividend yield and buybacks together with P/E.
List the risks and catalysts: rates, currency, energy, politics and policy.

Price divided by the last 12 months of actual earnings. The Nifty 50 was 20.20x on 4 September 2026.
(1 − P/E of cheaper market ÷ P/E of dearer market) × 100. Europe's discount to US stocks was about 26% in August 2026.
The part of a valuation gap explained by owning cheaper sectors, not by cheaper companies.
P/E divided by expected annual earnings growth in percent. Adjusts valuation for growth.
Return on equity. Net profit divided by shareholders' equity. Higher ROE supports a higher price-to-book ratio.
A stock or market that looks cheap but stays cheap, or gets cheaper, because of lasting structural problems.

points: In August 2026, the STOXX Europe 600 traded at about 14.6x forward earnings, a 26% discount to US stocks, narrowed from a record 41% in November 2024.
Always compare like with like: forward vs forward, trailing vs trailing, same source and date.
Sector mix explains much of the gap. The S&P 500 is 37.9% technology; MSCI Europe is 8.65% technology and 25.63% financials.
Slower long-term growth and lower average ROE justify part of Europe's lower valuation. Use PEG and P/B = ROE × P/E to test it.
US companies return cash mainly through buybacks (about $1 trillion in 2025); European companies lean more on dividends, though buybacks reached €182 billion in 2025.
Energy dependence, politics and rates add risk. The ECB raised its deposit rate to 2.50% from 16 September 2026.
Cheap is not the same as undervalued. Look for a catalyst before treating a discount as an opportunity.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Valuation, sector, buyback and interest rate data are drawn from LSEG I/B/E/S, FactSet, MSCI, S&P Dow Jones Indices, Morningstar, the ECB and published reports as of the dates stated, and may change. Sector P/Es, growth rates and ROE figures in the exercises are illustrative. Investing overseas from India is subject to LRS limits and tax rules. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any market or security.
